Decisions, with the options that lost

D2step 1 · understandfoundationopenby step

Do the 178 existing OS-specific sites in production code move behind the new platform layer?

A

Only new fleetd code uses the platform layer; existing sites stay

Pros
  • Smallest change
  • Matches the design's scope for the layer
Cons
  • 2 styles of OS code live side by side
Risks
  • Windows gaps in old code (Unix sockets, unknown machine probe) stay hidden
B

Move the existing sites that fleetd calls behind the layer as each phase touches them

Pros
  • Fleetd paths become first-class on all 3 OSes
  • Work is spread over the phases
Cons
  • Each phase grows
Risks
  • A phase gate covers less than the code it changes
C

Move all 178 sites behind the layer in 1 dedicated phase

Pros
  • 1 consistent rule enforced by arch_scan everywhere
Cons
  • A large change with no failure it fixes directly
Risks
  • Delays the phases that stop daily stalls
Would flip if
  • Windows is not used day to day
  • arch_scan can enforce the rule only on whole crates
  • A phase gate fails because of a moved site

waits on question Q2 answer: operator

D1step 2 · discoverboundaryopenmedium confidence

Where are the pivotal events that cut the fleetd timeline into phases?

A

4 pivotal events (assumptions approved, plan committed, task done, idea tasks landed) and 5 phases: clarifying, planning, executing, landing, integrating.

Pros
  • Each pivotal event is a state change of the design: approval gate, plan commit, verifier verdict, landed roll-up
  • Matches the actor changes in N7
Cons
  • Planning is a short phase with 5 events
Risks
  • Decompose may split planning from clarifying although 1 sub-orchestrator does both
B

2 pivotal events (assumptions approved, task done) and 3 phases: shaping, building, integrating.

Pros
  • Fewer, broader phases; the conservative reading
Cons
  • Hides the landing state machine inside building or integrating
  • Hides the plan commit, the moment a task can first exist
Risks
  • Landing and feature integration look like 1 context
C

5 pivotal events (add task done split from verification, so a separate verifying phase) and 6 phases.

Pros
  • Makes the verifier a visible phase, as the design stresses 'done is a fact on disk'
Cons
  • Verification interleaves with attempts (check failed loops back to an attempt), so the phase edge is not a before and after
Risks
  • Decompose cuts a verifier context that cannot decide alone
Would flip if
  • The operator treats planning as part of clarifying
  • The operator wants the verifier as its own phase

waits on question Q5 answer: operator

Is the verifier a context of its own, or a module of task-execution?

A

Module of task-execution: verification is an aggregate beside task and attempt.

Pros
  • 1 transaction for attempt end, verdict and task state
  • The skill tie-break says merge when the boundary is unsure
Cons
  • The judge rank language (CRITICAL, HIGH) sits beside lease language
Risks
  • task-execution grows large
B

Context of its own (verification) that task-execution calls after attempt-exited.

Pros
  • Matches the design component 'Verifier'
  • Keeps judge and review rules apart from dispatch
Cons
  • Every done needs a cross-context call and an event back
Risks
  • The reap and requeue rule 04 S7 spans 2 contexts
C

Merge verification into integration, since both run gates.

Pros
  • All gates in 1 place
Cons
  • Mixes task done with branch landed, which the design keeps apart (understand N4)
Risks
  • The word done changes meaning inside 1 model
Would flip if
  • The judge and review rules change on a different schedule from dispatch
  • Verification must run outside fleetd

Is worktree custody a context of its own, or a part of integration?

Own context worktree-custody.

D1step 4 · strategizeclassificationopenby stepmedium confidence

Is the ideas subdomain core or supporting?

A

Supporting, active-record: a flat idea state machine in code; the planning judgment stays in the sub-orchestrator model.

Pros
  • Keeps core the minority (2 of 6)
  • The dispatcher is deterministic and small by design (design, Ideas: the dispatcher and sub-orchestrators)
  • Spends aggregate design on the stall and landing rules, where the failures of today are
Cons
  • 24 events and 21 commands is a large state machine for active-record
  • Approval hash and 'no task outside a plan' are invariants a flat model can let slip
Risks
  • Plan validation rules grow and the flat model leaks them into callers
B

Core, domain-model: the idea and plan are aggregates with invariants (approval hash, 1 feature per idea, no task outside a validated plan).

Pros
  • G3 depends on it directly
  • Protects the C5 rule (only the operator approves) inside 1 aggregate
Cons
  • 3 of 6 subdomains core is not a minority
  • Much of the complexity is model work done by the sub-orchestrator, not fleetd code
Risks
  • Core budget is split 3 ways for 1 team
C

Split: plan validation is a supporting module with domain-model rules; idea intake and questions stay active-record.

Pros
  • Puts rich rules only where the invariants are
Cons
  • Decompose has 1 subdomain here; a split re-opens step 3
  • Adds a boundary nobody asked for
Risks
  • Re-runs decompose for a small gain
Would flip if
  • Plan validation rules turn out to need more than 1 aggregate
  • The operator names the idea pipeline as the reason to use fleetd
  • An idea bug, not a task stall, is the main failure in the first runs

recorded as assumption A1 Ideas is classified supporting, not core (decision D1 is open). Its 24 events are the transitions of 1 fixed idea state…

D2step 4 · strategizeclassificationopenby stepmedium confidence

Do the core subdomains use domain-model with an audit event table, or event-sourced-domain-model?

A

domain-model: state rows are the truth; transition() writes the row and 1 event in 1 transaction; events are audit.

Pros
  • Matches rule 1 One door literally (design, Ledger)
  • Reconciler reads rows each pass; no replay cost
  • Today's ledger is row-based (schema v7), so migration is smaller
Cons
  • 'Derived tables' in the design can be read as projections
Risks
  • Row and event can disagree if a bug writes one without the other
B

event-sourced-domain-model: the events table is the truth and the task, attempt, branch and feature tables are rebuilt from it.

Pros
  • Full history for forensic replay of a stall or a lost branch
  • Matches 'event log plus derived tables' read strictly
Cons
  • Replay and projection rebuild add work to every schema migration
  • The reconciler is level-triggered on rows, not on events
Risks
  • A failed migration that loses events loses state, not only history (05 L-4)
C

Mixed: event-sourced for task and attempt only, domain-model for integration.

Pros
  • History where the stall forensics need it
Cons
  • 2 persistence styles behind 1 door
Risks
  • Inconsistent transition() code paths
Would flip if
  • The operator needs 'state as of' queries for a past pass
  • The design means the derived tables are rebuilt from events
  • Row and event drift is seen in fault-injection tests

recorded as assumption A3 The 2 cores use domain-model: state rows are the truth, and the events table is the audit trail that the one door write…

D1step 1 · understandfoundationtakenby stephigh confidence

Is fleetd a change to horch or a new system that replaces it?

Achosen

Brownfield: fleetd is a set of changes to horch (keep, change, add)

Pros
  • Reuses the ledger, procid, herdr client, adapters and arch tests
  • Each phase keeps the fleet usable
Cons
  • Old shapes such as the v7 schema constrain the new model
Risks
  • A preserved behavior is dropped by accident
Why

The design says the design is a set of changes to horch, not a rewrite (Where multi-herdr stands today, Keep, change, add), and fleetd is a subcommand of the single horch binary (Amendment D9).

B

Rewrite: a new control plane that replaces horch

Pros
  • A clean model with no legacy shapes
Cons
  • Loses the preserved behaviors and the adapters
Risks
  • Lost work and a stuck fleet during the switch
C

Greenfield beside horch: a separate daemon that horch calls

Pros
  • Independent release
Cons
  • 2 versions of CLI and daemon can differ
Risks
  • Breaks C1: 1 binary, 1 version
Would flip if
  • The operator decides to fork horch into a new product

recorded as assumption A1 Lifecycle is brownfield: horch runs in production today, and the design is a set of changes to horch, not a rewrite (de…

TermMeans here

Its words5
TermMeans here
LeaseThe time-limited hold of 1 attempt on its task. It renews only on earned activity and pauses during sleep and waiting_quota (discover N1).
ReadyA task state: every dependency is done and the task waits for dispatch (discover N6).
DoneA task state that only the verifier sets, from facts on disk. It does not mean landed or merged (understand N4).
CheckThe acceptance command of a task. The verifier runs it in the worktree, in the sandbox profile of the worker.
FeatureA code kind of a task (with quality, refactor and security). It is not the feature of the integration context (discover N2).

Its words4
TermMeans here
Feature1 sub-orchestrator, 1 feature branch and 1 pull request to the primary branch, holding 1 main idea and its follow-on ideas (understand N2). The feature aggregate owns feature-opened to feature-merged (discover N2).
ReadyA task branch is ready when it is verified and waits for a bundle. A feature is ready when its full gate passed and its pull request can open (discover N6).
LandedA task branch state: the branch is fast-forwarded onto its feature branch after the fast gate passed (understand N4).
MergedA feature fact read from git by content: the feature branch is in the primary branch (understand N4).

The words

A word that means two things is where the parts were cut. Worth two minutes.

Every term38
TermWhereMeans
IdeaSharedA rough request from the operator that 1 fixed state machine moves from captured to merged; only code advances it. Avoid: ticket (a ticket enters as a --direct idea), request
FeatureShared1 sub-orchestrator, 1 feature branch and 1 pull request to the primary branch, holding 1 main idea and its follow-on ideas. The task kind 'feature' is a different thing (H2). Avoid: project, epic
Sub-OrchestratorSharedThe interactive Opus 5.5 agent of 1 feature that clarifies, specifies and plans 1 idea at a time, with a fresh process per phase. Avoid: orchestrator, lead
AssumptionShared1 line in assumptions.md, [confirmed] or [assumed], that the operator approves or revises; the sub-orchestrator can also record its own reversible one. Avoid: requirement
PlanSharedThe validated plan.yaml of 1 idea: tasks, dependencies, checks, paired judges. No task exists outside a committed plan. Avoid: ticket list
TaskSharedA planned unit of work from plan.yaml with a kind, a check and an owner path set; it survives many attempts (H1). Avoid: job, claim
AttemptShared1 run of 1 worker on 1 task (A1, A2, ...), launched through the wrapper and ended by fleetd. Avoid: run, session
LeaseSharedThe time-limited hold of an attempt on its task that renews only on earned activity and pauses during sleep and waiting_quota. Avoid: claim, lock
WorktreeSharedThe git working tree that fleetd leases to 1 task before it exists and never removes before its work is landed or rescued. Avoid: checkout, workspace
Rescue RefSharedA verified commit under refs/horch/rescue/ that saves the full state of a tree or an old branch tip before cleanup or rebase. Avoid: backup, archive ref (a different ref family)
Task BranchSharedThe branch of 1 task that lands on its feature branch through the landing state machine. Avoid: worker branch
Feature BranchSharedThe branch of 1 feature that collects its landed task branches and reaches the primary branch through 1 pull request. Avoid: integration branch
Primary BranchSharedThe base branch of a project; main in this repository, not in every project. Avoid: main, master, trunk
BundleShared1 candidate made from the feature branch tip plus every ready task branch of that feature, tested once by the fast gate. Avoid: batch, merge train
Fast GateSharedThe declared unit-test command of a project that every bundle and every rebased feature branch must pass. Avoid: CI, check
Full GateSharedThe fast gate plus the end-to-end tests, run on a feature tip over the current primary branch; a pass goes stale when either tip moves. Avoid: CI, e2e run
Trial MergeSharedA merge-tree result between 2 in-flight features, or a feature and the primary branch, recorded in the ledger with no checkout. Avoid: dry run
Resolver TaskSharedA code-kind task that resolves 1 conflict between stacked features, at most 100 changed lines or 2 files. Avoid: merge task
Judge TaskSharedA task of kind judge that ranks the misses of 1 judgment-kind task CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW; it needs no judge itself (H5). Avoid: review task, judgment task
FallbackSharedThe persona that a worker persona names for use when its provider pool shows a usage limit or an outage. Avoid: backup model
AssumptionIdeas context1 line in assumptions.md, [confirmed] or [assumed], that the operator approves or revises; also a reversible assumption that the sub-orchestrator records to answer a worker question (understand N11).
QuestionIdeas contextA worker question to the sub-orchestrator of its feature. It ends as an answer, an own assumption, a revise request, or an escalation to the operator.
OrchestratorIdeas contextNot a role in fleetd. The word survives only in the preserved mail contract tag [orchestrator re #<id>] (discover N3).
LeaseTask execution contextThe time-limited hold of 1 attempt on its task. It renews only on earned activity and pauses during sleep and waiting_quota (discover N1).
ReadyTask execution contextA task state: every dependency is done and the task waits for dispatch (discover N6).
DoneTask execution contextA task state that only the verifier sets, from facts on disk. It does not mean landed or merged (understand N4).
CheckTask execution contextThe acceptance command of a task. The verifier runs it in the worktree, in the sandbox profile of the worker.
FeatureTask execution contextA code kind of a task (with quality, refactor and security). It is not the feature of the integration context (discover N2).
LeaseWorktree custody contextThe worktree lease: the ledger row written in the same transaction that leases the task, before the directory exists. It holds the worktree for 1 task until its work is landed or rescued.
LandedWorktree custody contextA worktree state: nothing in the worktree is unique any more, so fleetd may remove it (discover N6).
OrphanedWorktree custody contextA worktree on disk with no live owner attempt, or with no ledger row.
FeatureLanding and integration context1 sub-orchestrator, 1 feature branch and 1 pull request to the primary branch, holding 1 main idea and its follow-on ideas (understand N2). The feature aggregate owns feature-opened to feature-merged (discover N2).
ReadyLanding and integration contextA task branch is ready when it is verified and waits for a bundle. A feature is ready when its full gate passed and its pull request can open (discover N6).
LandedLanding and integration contextA task branch state: the branch is fast-forwarded onto its feature branch after the fast gate passed (understand N4).
MergedLanding and integration contextA feature fact read from git by content: the feature branch is in the primary branch (understand N4).
ProfileWorker profiles and adapters contextA named worker profile: the CLI, model, effort, sandbox and permission rules that 1 attempt runs with.
HealthyWorker profiles and adapters contextA profile whose adapter passed its last conformance test. Dispatch does not choose an unhealthy profile.
CheckFleet runtime contexthorch fleetd check: the heartbeat check that restarts fleetd when its last full pass is older than 30 s of awake time. It is not a task check.

Step by step, in plain words

Each step in four sentences: what it did, what it decided, what it guessed, and what hurts most if the guess is wrong.

1understanddone2 on the listWhy the system should exist and who it is for.
what
We wrote down why fleetd exists, who it serves, what counts as success and how big it may get.
decided
fleetd is a change to horch, not a new product. It ships inside the 1 horch binary, for 1 operator and 1 team. Success is 4 numbers: idle tasks caught in under 10 minutes, 0 lost work, 0 tasks outside an approved plan, 0 attempts burned by usage limits.
assumed
The design gives no number for using the subscription fully, so we used a proxy: no usage window resets with usage left while work is ready.
riskiest
If the proxy for full usage is wrong, later steps may build pacing toward the wrong target. The 178 old OS-specific code sites are also still undecided, which affects how first-class Windows really is.

10 guesses · 8 open questions · 17 notes forward · 2 decisions

  "constraints": [
    {
      "id": "C1",
      "kind": "technical",
      "text": "fleetd is a subcommand of the single horch binary: 1 deployable unit, so the CLI and the daemon always have the same version"
    },
    {
      "id": "C2",
      "kind": "organisational",
      "text": "Absolute operator rule: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is never used and is removed from every child process, pane command line, detached child, updater and probe; every claude run uses the subscription login. agy children lose GEMINI_API_KEY, GOOGLE_API_KEY and GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL"
    },
    {
      "id": "C3",
      "kind": "technical",
      "text": "macOS, Linux and Windows are first-class hosts. Core fleetd code has no cfg(target_os), cfg(unix) or cfg(windows); it calls 1 platform interface with 1 module per OS, and an OS without an equivalent returns an explicit not-supported value"
    },
    {
      "id": "C4",
      "kind": "technical",
      "text": "Exactly 1 process writes the ledger (SQLite in WAL mode, ~/.horch/ledger.sqlite3). Schema migration is forward-only at daemon start, a backup is written first (3 kept), a newer schema is refused, and a development build does not migrate the shared ledger"
    },
    {
      "id": "C5",
      "kind": "organisational",
      "text": "Only the operator approves an idea's assumptions, with a command run outside any fleet process; a model can never approve for the operator"
    },
    {
      "id": "C6",
      "kind": "technical",
      "text": "fleetd keeps the behaviors of the Preservation analysis, among them 04 W6, F9, F7, F5, L5, L9, W8, W9, F11, S7, L6, L8, S8, S10 and M5"
    },
    {
      "id": "C7",
      "kind": "technical",
      "text": "fleetd keeps the contract surface: exit codes 0, 1, 2 and 3, the mail contract for interactive panes, the UNLANDED and UNREGISTERED reports, horch self-update and its release assets, ticket format C1 and project facts"
    },
    {
      "id": "C8",
      "kind": "technical",
      "text": "fleetd keeps today's fixed values: land lock 1 h with 5 tries, check timeout 20 min (max 24 h), git push 10 min and other git network calls 3 min, code-sweep at most 2 requeues and review rounds of 1 (light) and 3 (full)"
    },
    {
      "id": "C9",
      "kind": "timeline",
      "text": "Migration runs in 8 phases (0 to 7) in order. Each phase is released to every user at once when its fault-injection tests pass; the tests are the only gate"
    },
    {
      "id": "C10",
      "kind": "contractual",
      "text": "Agent CLI vendors set the terms: each provider pool has a usage window and limits, Codex user hooks need trust, and a new CLI release is used only after the update cooldown of more than 1 week"
    },
    {
      "id": "C11",
      "kind": "technical",
      "text": "The only bytes typed into a terminal are 1 fixed doorbell line written by fleetd's code; all hand-off between agents is through files written atomically"
    },
    {
      "id": "C12",
      "kind": "technical",
      "text": "Each agent works inside a context limit of 256k tokens"
    },
    {
      "id": "C13",
      "kind": "budget",
      "text": "There is no spend budget and no cap on features, sub-orchestrators or workers. Only health guards for free disk and machine load pause new dispatch"
    },
    {
      "id": "C14",
      "kind": "technical",
      "text": "herdr holds no state that fleetd depends on; after a herdr restart fleetd rebuilds from the ledger and the files"
    }
  ],

2discoverdone7 on the listEverything that happens in the business, named.
what
This step lists, in time order, everything that happens to 1 idea in fleetd: from 'horch idea add' to the feature merged in the primary branch, with the people and programs that cause each step.
decided
The flow has 5 phases cut at 4 moments: the operator approves the assumptions, the plan commits, the verifier marks a task done, and every task of the idea lands on its feature branch.
assumed
The daemon restart and adapter checks fit at the end of task execution, and a feature is opened only when the first assumptions exist. Both are open for the operator.
riskiest
The words 'ready', 'landed' and 'done' each mean 2 or 3 different states. If later steps merge them, a status can say work is safe when it has not reached the primary branch.

10 guesses · 5 open questions · 8 notes forward · 2 decisions

  "policies": [
    {
      "id": "start-lead-on-capture",
      "name": "Whenever an idea is captured, start a sub-orchestrator for its feature",
      "when": "idea-captured",
      "then": [
        "start-sub-orchestrator"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "open-feature-on-assumptions",
      "name": "Whenever assumptions are written for an idea with no feature branch, open the feature",
      "when": "assumptions-written",
      "then": [
        "open-feature"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "request-approval-on-feature",
      "name": "Whenever the feature of an idea with valid assumptions is open, request approval",
      "when": "feature-opened",
      "then": [
        "request-approval"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "restart-lead-on-revise",
      "name": "Whenever assumptions are revised, start a fresh sub-orchestrator in clarifying",
      "when": "assumptions-revised",
      "then": [
        "start-sub-orchestrator"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "park-on-unanswered-approval",
      "name": "Whenever approval is requested and 7 days pass with no answer, park the idea",
      "when": "approval-requested",
      "then": [
        "park-idea"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "specify-on-approval",
      "name": "Whenever assumptions are approved, start a fresh sub-orchestrator in specifying",
      "when": "assumptions-approved",
      "then": [
        "start-sub-orchestrator"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "open-feature-on-direct",
      "name": "Whenever a direct idea with no --to is accepted, open a feature named from the ticket title",
      "when": "direct-idea-accepted",
      "then": [
        "open-feature"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "validate-on-plan-submitted",
      "name": "Whenever a plan is submitted, validate it",
      "when": "plan-submitted",
      "then": [
        "validate-plan"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "escalate-on-plan-refused",
      "name": "Whenever a direct plan is refused, escalate it to needs-you",
      "when": "plan-refused",
      "then": [
        "escalate-task"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "promote-on-plan-committed",
      "name": "Whenever a plan is committed, promote the tasks with no dependencies",
      "when": "plan-committed",
      "then": [
        "promote-task"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "dispatch-on-ready",
      "name": "Whenever a task is ready, dispatch it unless a health guard or pacing holds it",
      "when": "task-promoted",
      "then": [
        "dispatch-task"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "create-worktree-on-lease",
      "name": "Whenever a task is leased, create its worktree unless one exists",
      "when": "task-leased",
      "then": [
        "create-worktree"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "launch-on-worktree",
      "name": "Whenever a worktree is created for a leased task, launch the attempt",
      "when": "worktree-created",
      "then": [
        "launch-attempt"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "end-on-stall",
      "name": "Whenever an attempt stalls, end the attempt",
      "when": "attempt-stalled",
      "then": [
        "end-attempt"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "end-on-lease-expired",
      "name": "Whenever a lease expires, end the attempt",
      "when": "lease-expired",
      "then": [
        "end-attempt"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "fallback-on-usage-limit",
      "name": "Whenever a usage limit is reported, move the task to its fallback or to waiting_quota",
      "when": "usage-limit-reported",
      "then": [
        "move-to-fallback"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "launch-on-fallback",
      "name": "Whenever a task moves to its fallback, launch a new attempt on the same worktree",
      "when": "fallback-assigned",
      "then": [
        "launch-attempt"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "promote-on-quota-reset",
      "name": "Whenever a quota window resets, promote the tasks waiting on that pool",
      "when": "quota-window-reset",
      "then": [
        "promote-task"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "start-owner-on-question",
      "name": "Whenever a worker asks a question, start its owner sub-orchestrator until an answer is recorded",
      "when": "worker-question-asked",
      "then": [
        "start-sub-orchestrator"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "resume-on-answer",
      "name": "Whenever a question is answered, resume the worker session with the answer",
      "when": "question-answered",
      "then": [
        "launch-attempt"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "resume-on-own-assumption",
      "name": "Whenever the sub-orchestrator records its own assumption, resume the worker session",
      "when": "own-assumption-recorded",
      "then": [
        "launch-attempt"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "operator-decides-revise",
      "name": "Whenever a revise is requested, the operator approves or revises the changed assumption",
      "when": "revise-requested",
      "then": [
        "approve-assumptions",
        "revise-assumptions"
      ],
      "kind": "manual"
    },
    {
      "id": "verify-on-exit",
      "name": "Whenever an attempt exits with a result, run its check",
      "when": "attempt-exited",
      "then": [
        "run-check"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "repair-on-exit-without-result",
      "name": "Whenever an attempt exits with commits and no result, resume once to write the result",
      "when": "attempt-exited",
      "then": [
        "write-result"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "review-on-check-passed",
      "name": "Whenever the check of a code-kind task passes, run the review scripts",

      "then": [
        "run-review"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "done-on-judge-check",
      "name": "Whenever the structural check of a judge task passes, mark it done",

      "then": [

      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "end-on-check-failed",
      "name": "Whenever a check fails, end the attempt as failed",
      "when": "check-failed",
      "then": [
        "end-attempt"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "done-on-review-passed",
      "name": "Whenever the review passes, mark the task done",
      "when": "review-passed",

        "mark-task-done"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "end-on-review-failed",
      "name": "Whenever the review fails, end the attempt as failed",
      "when": "review-failed",
      "then": [
        "end-attempt"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "settle-judge-verdict",
      "name": "Whenever a judge verdict is written, mark the judged task done with no CRITICAL, else open a fix",
      "when": "judge-verdict-written",
      "then": [
        "mark-task-done",
        "open-critical-fix"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "lead-settles-high",
      "name": "Whenever a judge verdict has a HIGH finding, the sub-orchestrator fixes or dismisses it",
      "when": "judge-verdict-written",
      "then": [
        "settle-high-finding"
      ],
      "kind": "manual"
    },
    {
      "id": "escalate-after-two-fixes",
      "name": "Whenever a second critical fix still leaves a CRITICAL item, escalate the task",
      "when": "critical-fix-opened",
      "then": [
        "escalate-task"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "retry-on-attempt-failed",
      "name": "Whenever an attempt fails, retry after backoff or request a replan",
      "when": "attempt-failed",
      "then": [
        "schedule-retry"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "launch-on-retry",
      "name": "Whenever a retry is scheduled, launch the next attempt in the same worktree after backoff",
      "when": "retry-scheduled",
      "then": [
        "launch-attempt"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "lead-replans-on-request",
      "name": "Whenever a replan is requested, the sub-orchestrator replans the task once",
      "when": "replan-requested",
      "then": [
        "replan-task"
      ],
      "kind": "manual"
    },
    {
      "id": "promote-on-replan",
      "name": "Whenever a task is replanned, promote it",
      "when": "task-replanned",
      "then": [
        "promote-task"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "promote-on-requeue",
      "name": "Whenever the operator requeues a task, promote it",
      "when": "task-requeued",
      "then": [
        "promote-task"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "rescue-on-orphan",
      "name": "Whenever a worktree is orphaned, rescue it before any cleanup",

        "rescue-worktree"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "escalate-on-rescue-failed",
      "name": "Whenever a rescue fails verification, escalate",
      "when": "rescue-failed",
      "then": [
        "escalate-task"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "ready-branch-on-done",
      "name": "Whenever a task is done, mark its task branch ready",

    {

      "kind": "automatic"

      "id": "restart-on-binary-change",
      "name": "Whenever the horch binary is updated, restart fleetd on the new binary",

      "then": [
        "restart-fleetd"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"

      "id": "block-profile-on-conformance",
      "name": "Whenever adapter conformance fails, mark the profile unhealthy",

      "then": [
        "mark-profile-unhealthy"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "bundle-on-ready",
      "name": "Whenever a task branch is ready, add it to the next bundle of its feature",

      "then": [
        "build-bundle"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "gate-on-bundle",
      "name": "Whenever a bundle is built, run the fast gate on it",

      "then": [
        "run-fast-gate"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "relaunch-on-conflict",
      "name": "Whenever a task branch conflicts, the same worker resolves the rebase",

      "then": [
        "launch-attempt"

      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "land-on-fast-gate-pass",
      "name": "Whenever the fast gate passes, fast-forward the feature branch",
      "when": "fast-gate-passed",
      "then": [
        "fast-forward-feature-branch"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "bisect-on-fast-gate-fail",
      "name": "Whenever the fast gate fails, bisect the bundle",
      "when": "fast-gate-failed",
      "then": [
        "bisect-bundle"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "triage-on-gate-failed",
      "name": "Whenever a task branch fails the gate, open a triage task",
      "when": "task-branch-gate-failed",
      "then": [
        "open-triage-task"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "after-landing",
      "name": "Whenever a task branch lands, remove its worktree, roll up the idea and run trial merges",
      "when": "task-branch-landed",
      "then": [
        "remove-worktree",
        "roll-up-idea",
        "run-trial-merges"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "full-gate-on-landed",
      "name": "Whenever every task of an idea is landed, run the full gate of its feature",
      "when": "idea-tasks-landed",
      "then": [
        "run-full-gate"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "on-primary-moved",
      "name": "Whenever the primary branch moves, rebase each feature branch and run trial merges",
      "when": "primary-branch-moved",
      "then": [
        "rebase-feature-branch",
        "run-trial-merges"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "stack-on-conflict",
      "name": "Whenever a trial merge of 2 features conflicts, stack the younger feature on the older one",
      "when": "trial-merge-conflicted",
      "then": [
        "stack-feature"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "resolve-on-stack",
      "name": "Whenever a feature is stacked, open 1 resolver task",
      "when": "feature-stacked",
      "then": [
        "open-resolver-task"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "resolve-on-rebase-conflict",
      "name": "Whenever a feature rebase conflicts, open a resolver task",
      "when": "feature-rebase-conflicted",
      "then": [
        "open-resolver-task"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "gate-on-rebase",
      "name": "Whenever a feature branch is rebased, run the fast gate again",
      "when": "feature-branch-rebased",
      "then": [
        "run-fast-gate"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "ready-on-full-gate",
      "name": "Whenever the full gate passes, mark the feature ready",
      "when": "full-gate-passed",
      "then": [
        "mark-feature-ready"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "triage-on-full-gate-failed",
      "name": "Whenever the full gate fails, open triage tasks of the feature",
      "when": "full-gate-failed",
      "then": [
        "open-triage-task"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "pr-on-ready",
      "name": "Whenever a feature is ready, push it and open its pull request",
      "when": "feature-marked-ready",
      "then": [
        "open-pull-request"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "operator-merges",
      "name": "Whenever a pull request is opened, the operator reviews and merges it",
      "when": "pull-request-opened",
      "then": [
        "merge-pull-request"
      ],
      "kind": "manual"
    },
    {
      "id": "close-on-feature-merged",
      "name": "Whenever a feature is merged, close each of its ideas once their worktrees are removed",
      "when": "feature-merged",
      "then": [
        "close-idea"
      ],
      "kind": "automatic"
    },
    {
      "id": "operator-decides-escalation",
      "name": "Whenever a task is escalated, the operator requeues or abandons it",
      "when": "task-escalated",
      "then": [
        "requeue-task",
        "abandon-task-branch"
      ],
      "kind": "manual"
    }
  ],

  "pivotal_events": [
    "assumptions-approved",
    "plan-committed",
    "task-done",
    "idea-tasks-landed"

  "hotspots": [
    {
      "id": "H1",
      "kind": "conflict",
      "near": "attempt-launched",
      "text": "Today a worker 'claims' a task and the 'task' row carries the run; fleetd splits this into task (planned unit from plan.yaml), attempt (1 run of 1 worker: A1, A2) and lease (the time-limited hold that renews only on earned activity). Readers of today's ledger and code will read 'task' where fleetd means 'attempt' (understand N1)."
    },
    {
      "id": "H2",
      "kind": "conflict",
      "near": "feature-opened",
      "text": "'Feature' is also a task kind (kind: feature, a code kind) and a word for any change. In fleetd a Feature is 1 sub-orchestrator, 1 feature branch and 1 pull request holding 1 main idea and its follow-on ideas. Which meaning does each document use (understand N2)?"
    },
    {
      "id": "H3",
      "kind": "conflict",
      "near": "sub-orchestrator-started",
      "text": "'Orchestrator' today is 1 long-lived LLM conversation that receives ideas, creates tasks and reads mail. In fleetd it does not exist: a deterministic idea dispatcher and 1 sub-orchestrator per feature replace it. Today's mail contract still names [orchestrator re #<id>] answers (understand N3)."
    },
    {
      "id": "H4",
      "kind": "conflict",
      "near": "task-done",
      "text": "'Done' today is a model action (horch ledger done / horch done). In fleetd only the verifier moves a task to done, and 'landed' (on the feature branch) and 'merged' (in the primary branch by content) are later, separate facts. A reader can take 'done' to mean the work reached the primary branch (understand N4)."
    },
    {
      "id": "H5",
      "kind": "conflict",
      "near": "judge-verdict-written",
      "text": "'Judgment kind' (research, design, docs, report, creative) and the kind 'judge' sound alike. A judgment task needs a paired judge task; a judge task needs no judge. A resolver task has a code kind. Mixing them breaks plan validation (understand N12)."
    },
    {
      "id": "H6",
      "kind": "conflict",
      "near": "task-branch-verified",
      "text": "'Ready' names 3 states: a task is ready when its dependencies are done (not yet dispatched); a task branch is ready when it is verified and waits for a bundle; a feature is ready when its full gate passed. 'Landed' is both a task branch state and a worktree state. Which one does a status line mean?"
    },
    {
      "id": "H7",
      "kind": "unclear",
      "near": "idea-captured",
      "text": "The idea row records its feature (ideas.feature_id), but the feature row and branch are written when the sub-orchestrator first writes assumptions. Which feature does an idea with no --to point at between capture and assumptions, and what does horch ideas show for it?"
    },
    {
      "id": "H8",
      "kind": "risk",
      "near": "task-branch-landed",
      "text": "The Preservation analysis rows (04 W6, F9, F7, F5, L5, L9, W8, W9, F11, S7, L6, L8, S8, S10, M5, 05 E-10, 06 S1 to S15) are hard inputs. Each must have exactly 1 owner in the model; a row that falls between 2 owners is a behavior fleetd silently drops (understand N15)."
    },
    {
      "id": "H9",
      "kind": "unclear",
      "near": "task-leased",
      "text": "What number counts as 'full use' of the subscription usage that pacing aims for? Pacing holds dispatch per pool window, but the design gives no target (understand Q1)."
    },
    {
      "id": "H10",
      "kind": "unclear",
      "near": "question-escalated",
      "text": "A worker question has 'a time limit' before it escalates, but the design gives no value for it, and it does not say if the limit pauses while the operator is outside working hours."
    },
    {
      "id": "H11",
      "kind": "external",
      "near": "fast-gate-passed",
      "text": "Plan validation refuses a project that has not declared a fast gate and a full gate, and this repository has no unit-only command today (research-03 F10, understand Q8). Until one is declared, no plan of this repository can commit."
    },
    {
      "id": "H12",
      "kind": "unclear",
      "near": "task-requeued",
      "text": "A task gets max_attempts attempts, then 1 replan, then goes to the operator. A requeue resets attempt_floor (04 L8). Does a requeued task also get a new replan, and how does the 2-requeue limit of the review scripts count against attempts?"
    },
    {
      "id": "H13",
      "kind": "risk",
      "near": "lease-expired",
      "text": "Lease and stall time count only while the machine is awake. If the platform layer reports sleep and wake wrongly on 1 OS, leases expire during a sleep and every worker burns an attempt at wake."
    },
    {
      "id": "H14",
      "kind": "missing",
      "near": "adapter-conformance-failed",
      "text": "Docs sync and adapter conformance are collapsed to 2 events here. The flow that turns a drift into a task (who owns it, how a profile becomes healthy again) is not stormed."
    },
    {
      "id": "H15",
      "kind": "external",
      "near": "pull-request-merged",
      "text": "A project setting says who merges a feature; the default is the operator. When the setting lets fleetd merge, which gate and which actor stands for the merge decision?"
    }
  ],

  "glossary": [
    {
      "term": "Idea",
      "definition": "A rough request from the operator that 1 fixed state machine moves from captured to merged; only code advances it.",
      "avoid": [
        "ticket (a ticket enters as a --direct idea)",
        "request"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Feature",
      "definition": "1 sub-orchestrator, 1 feature branch and 1 pull request to the primary branch, holding 1 main idea and its follow-on ideas. The task kind 'feature' is a different thing (H2).",
      "avoid": [
        "project",
        "epic"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Sub-Orchestrator",
      "definition": "The interactive Opus 5.5 agent of 1 feature that clarifies, specifies and plans 1 idea at a time, with a fresh process per phase.",
      "avoid": [
        "orchestrator",
        "lead"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Assumption",
      "definition": "1 line in assumptions.md, [confirmed] or [assumed], that the operator approves or revises; the sub-orchestrator can also record its own reversible one.",
      "avoid": [
        "requirement"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Plan",
      "definition": "The validated plan.yaml of 1 idea: tasks, dependencies, checks, paired judges. No task exists outside a committed plan.",
      "avoid": [
        "ticket list"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Task",
      "definition": "A planned unit of work from plan.yaml with a kind, a check and an owner path set; it survives many attempts (H1).",
      "avoid": [
        "job",
        "claim"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Attempt",
      "definition": "1 run of 1 worker on 1 task (A1, A2, ...), launched through the wrapper and ended by fleetd.",
      "avoid": [
        "run",
        "session"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Lease",
      "definition": "The time-limited hold of an attempt on its task that renews only on earned activity and pauses during sleep and waiting_quota.",
      "avoid": [
        "claim",
        "lock"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Worktree",
      "definition": "The git working tree that fleetd leases to 1 task before it exists and never removes before its work is landed or rescued.",
      "avoid": [
        "checkout",
        "workspace"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Rescue Ref",
      "definition": "A verified commit under refs/horch/rescue/ that saves the full state of a tree or an old branch tip before cleanup or rebase.",
      "avoid": [
        "backup",
        "archive ref (a different ref family)"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Task Branch",
      "definition": "The branch of 1 task that lands on its feature branch through the landing state machine.",
      "avoid": [
        "worker branch"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Feature Branch",
      "definition": "The branch of 1 feature that collects its landed task branches and reaches the primary branch through 1 pull request.",
      "avoid": [
        "integration branch"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Primary Branch",
      "definition": "The base branch of a project; main in this repository, not in every project.",
      "avoid": [
        "main",
        "master",
        "trunk"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Bundle",
      "definition": "1 candidate made from the feature branch tip plus every ready task branch of that feature, tested once by the fast gate.",
      "avoid": [
        "batch",
        "merge train"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Fast Gate",
      "definition": "The declared unit-test command of a project that every bundle and every rebased feature branch must pass.",
      "avoid": [
        "CI",
        "check"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Full Gate",
      "definition": "The fast gate plus the end-to-end tests, run on a feature tip over the current primary branch; a pass goes stale when either tip moves.",
      "avoid": [
        "CI",
        "e2e run"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Trial Merge",
      "definition": "A merge-tree result between 2 in-flight features, or a feature and the primary branch, recorded in the ledger with no checkout.",
      "avoid": [
        "dry run"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Resolver Task",
      "definition": "A code-kind task that resolves 1 conflict between stacked features, at most 100 changed lines or 2 files.",
      "avoid": [
        "merge task"
      ],
      "context": null
    },
    {
      "term": "Judge Task",
      "definition": "A task of kind judge that ranks the misses of 1 judgment-kind task CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW; it needs no judge itself (H5).",
      "avoid": [
        "review task",

    },

3decomposedone8 on the listWhere the lines are drawn between the parts.
what
This step cut fleetd into 6 parts, each with its own words and its own data: ideas, task execution, worktree custody, landing and integration, worker profiles, and the fleet runtime.
decided
6 parts, all modules inside the 1 horch binary, joined by 13 named links. Each of the 82 events and 64 commands has exactly 1 owner.
assumed
The verifier lives inside task execution, and worker questions live inside ideas. Both are open decisions for the operator (D1, D2).
riskiest
If worker profiles is not its own part, the rule that strips ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from every launch has no single owner, and 1 missed launch path bills the API key.

9 guesses · 3 open questions · 6 notes forward · 4 decisions

4strategizedone2 on the listWhich parts are worth our best effort, and which to buy.
what
We decided which parts of fleetd need the most careful design, and which parts stay simple.
decided
2 of 6 parts are core: running and checking tasks, and landing branches on features. The other 4 parts are built simply. We buy nothing new. herdr and the OS service managers are used as they are.
assumed
The ideas part is not core, because an AI does its hard thinking and the code is 1 fixed state machine. We also assumed the ledger rows are the truth and the events table is an audit log.
riskiest
If plan checks in the ideas part grow into many rules, the simple design there will leak bugs, and a task could start without an approved plan.

system5record
name
fleetd: the horch fleet control plane
one_liner
A supervised daemon inside horch that takes rough ideas from the operator, runs AI coding agents on them, and keeps every task, worktree and branch accounted for until the work reaches the primary branch.
problem
The operator runs a fleet of AI coding agents with horch. Tasks get forgotten, workers do not find work or sit idle on it, finished work is never reported, the watchdog misses updates, stacked ideas merge in one orchestrator conversation, and dead workers leave orphaned worktrees. Each failure comes from a job that horch still leaves to an LLM.
why_now
Daily stalls and lost worktrees cost subscription usage and operator attention. horch already has the parts (recorded PIDs, a supervisor per worker, worktrees per task, finish steps), and a design review on 2026-11-11 and 2026-11-12 approved the design.
lifecycle
brownfield
business_model10record
customer_segments
The operator: a solo developer who runs a fleet of AI coding agents on 1 machine Friends who install horch and get new releases through horch self-update
value_propositions
No task stalls silently: every task ends verified done or escalated with a reason No paid-for work is lost: every worktree and branch is known and rescued before removal Rough ideas in, approved plans out: 1 idea at a time, nothing built before approval The subscription usage is used fully across agent CLIs and providers Parallel features reach the primary branch through 1 pull request each, with conflicts found early
channels
The horch CLI (horch idea add, horch ideas, horch status, horch idea approve) herdr panes, the herdr sidebar and herdr notifications The needs-you folder GitHub releases and horch self-update
customer_relationships
Self-service from the terminal An interview with the operator in the pane of each sub-orchestrator Quick approval of written assumptions by the operator
revenue_streams
None: horch is the operator's own tool; the return is operator throughput (assumed)
key_resources
The ledger (1 SQLite file, 1 writer) The files of the fleet workspace (ideas, tasks, attempts, rescue manifests) Git repositories, worktrees and rescue refs The worker profiles in teammates/ Subscription usage of each provider pool The host machine: disk, CPU and memory
key_activities
Dispatch ideas through a fixed state machine Plan 1 idea at a time with operator approval Bind tasks to workers and supervise attempts with leases Verify each task on disk Lease, reconcile and rescue worktrees Land task branches and integrate features Pace dispatch to each usage window Keep each agent CLI adapter conformant
key_partners
herdr (pane runtime) Agent CLI vendors: Anthropic (Claude Code), OpenAI (Codex CLI), Google (Antigravity), OpenCode, pi, Prime OS service managers: launchd, systemd, Windows services and Task Scheduler GitHub (releases, gh for pull requests)
cost_structure
Subscription usage of each provider pool Machine resources: disk for worktrees, CPU and memory for agent processes Operator attention for interviews, approvals and escalations

rationale
Recommendation: B. The design makes Windows first-class (D1) but keeps the migration of existing sites as a separate decision. Moving the sites that fleetd calls, as each phase touches them, closes the Windows gaps that matter to fleetd without a big-bang phase. Strongest argument against: it blurs each phase's fault-injection gate with refactoring work.

Today a worker 'claims' a task and the 'task' row carries the run; fleetd splits this into task (planned unit from plan.yaml), attempt (1 run of 1 worker: A1, A2) and lease (the time-limited hold that renews only on earned activity). Readers of today's ledger and code will read 'task' where fleetd means 'attempt' (understand N1).

'Orchestrator' today is 1 long-lived LLM conversation that receives ideas, creates tasks and reads mail. In fleetd it does not exist: a deterministic idea dispatcher and 1 sub-orchestrator per feature replace it. Today's mail contract still names [orchestrator re #<id>] answers (understand N3).

In fleetd only the verifier moves a task to done, and 'landed' (on the feature branch) and 'merged' (in the primary branch by content) are later, separate facts. A reader can take 'done' to mean the work reached the primary branch (understand N4).

4 pivotal events (assumptions approved, plan committed, task done, idea tasks landed) and 5 phases: clarifying, planning, executing, landing, integrating.

pros
Each pivotal event is a state change of the design: approval gate, plan commit, verifier verdict, landed roll-up Matches the actor changes in N7
cons
Planning is a short phase with 5 events

B 2 pivotal events (assumptions approved, task done) and 3 phases: shaping, building, integrating.

Landing and feature integration look like 1 context

Referenced nowhere else.

C 5 pivotal events (add task done split from verification, so a separate verifying phase) and 6 phases.
pros
Makes the verifier a visible phase, as the design stresses 'done is a fact on disk'
cons
Verification interleaves with attempts (check failed loops back to an attempt), so the phase edge is not a before and after
risks
Decompose cuts a verifier context that cannot decide alone

Recommendation: A. The design names an approval gate, a plan commit, a verifier verdict and a landed roll-up as distinct facts. Strongest argument against A: clarifying and planning are 1 sub-orchestrator on 1 idea folder, so the cut between them may not be a context boundary.

Cut at the pivotal events assumptions-approved and plan-committed (pivotal-event) and by the actor change: operator and sub-orchestrator own clarifying and planning (discover N7). Lease
meaning_here
The time-limited hold of 1 attempt on its task. It renews only on earned activity and pauses during sleep and waiting_quota (discover N1).
Ready
meaning_here
A task state: every dependency is done and the task waits for dispatch (discover N6).
Done
meaning_here
A task state that only the verifier sets, from facts on disk. It does not mean landed or merged (understand N4).
Check
meaning_here
The acceptance command of a task. The verifier runs it in the worktree, in the sandbox profile of the worker.
Feature
meaning_here
A code kind of a task (with quality, refactor and security). It is not the feature of the integration context (discover N2).

verdict
candidate
rationale
Cut between plan-committed and task-done (pivotal-event). Task, attempt and verification are 3 aggregate candidates with 1 shared language (task, attempt, lease, done) and 1 transaction rule: a reap ends the attempt and requeues the task in 1 transaction (04 S7). The verifier is a separate component in the design, but it reads and writes the same task states, so it stays a module here (decision D1). The context adapts the agent CLI process (attempt-exited, through the fleet-run wrapper) and the provider pools (usage-limit-reported, quota-window-reset); both adapters are internal.

whatWe decided which parts of fleetd need the most careful design, and which parts stay simple.
decided2 of 6 parts are core: running and checking tasks, and landing branches on features. The other 4 parts are built simply. We buy nothing new. herdr and the OS service managers are used as they are.
assumedThe ideas part is not core, because an AI does its hard thinking and the code is 1 fixed state machine. We also assumed the ledger rows are the truth and the events table is an audit log.
riskiestIf plan checks in the ideas part grow into many rules, the simple design there will leak bugs, and a task could start without an approved plan.

Decisive core (both scores >= 8): the big investment, aggregates for task, attempt and verification with invariant tests for I1, I2 and I4. Review in 6 to 12 months; usage pacing can move to supporting once the pacing rule is stable (bet B3).

summarystring
2 of 6 subdomains are core: task-execution (decisive) and integration. Ideas, worktree-custody, worker-profiles and fleet-runtime are supporting and built simply. Nothing is generic: herdr and the OS service managers are adopted inside fleet-runtime as adapters. Every subdomain is built in horch-core; 2 classification calls (D1, D2) stay open for the operator.

Everything the run guessed or asked

36 guesses and 18 open questions across 4 steps.

Every guess36
StepidSure?The guess
understandA1highLifecycle is brownfield: horch runs in production today, and the design is a set of changes to horch, not a rewrite (design.md, Where multi-herdr stands today, Keep, change, add).
understandA2mediumThe operator is the single primary actor. Friends who install horch through horch self-update are a secondary segment with the same needs and no approval role.
understandA3mediumhorch earns no revenue. Its value is operator throughput: approved ideas that reach the primary branch per unit of subscription usage.
understandA4lowThe design gives no number for full use of the subscription usage. G4 uses a proxy: no pool ends its window with usage left while a task is ready, and a usage limit burns 0 attempts.
understandA5mediumA judge, a resolver and a triage agent are workers that run a task of a given kind. They are not separate actors.
understandA6mediumEvolution stages: the control-plane capabilities are custom because no product does them for local agent CLIs; pane hosting is a product (herdr); host platform services are a commodity (each OS provides them).
understandA7mediumThe alternatives are inferred from the design and the research files: today's horch with 1 orchestrator conversation, agents run by hand, and hosted merge queues (GitHub merge queue, bors, Mergify).
understandA8highThe /fleet paths in the design are a neutral layout. In horch, /fleet/ideas/<id>/ is ai_docs/plans/<run>/, /fleet/tasks/ is under the state root, and the ledger stays at ~/.horch/ledger.sqlite3.
understandA9highWhen the design and another source disagree, the design wins. The other sources describe the system of today.
understandA10highMode auto, depth standard, 1 deployable unit and 1 team are fixed by the run. The operator and the AI agents of the fleet count as 1 team.
discoverA1highThe board is to-be: it models fleetd as design.md describes it, not today's horch. Today's differences appear as conflict hotspots H1 to H4 (design.md wins over the other sources, per the run context).
discoverA2mediumThe 5 phases and 4 pivotal events are a hypothesis drawn from the idea state machine (captured to merged) and the landing state machine. Decision D1 records the alternatives.
discoverA3mediumDaemon supervision (stale heartbeat, restart, self-update) and adapter conformance are cross-cutting. They sit at the end of the executing phase (sequence 540 to 580, before Task Done) because they act on running attempts. Decision D2 records the alternatives.
discoverA4highfleetd components (idea dispatcher, verifier, landing, wrapper, reconciler) are our own system, not actors. Their commands have actor null and are issued by policies, or have the clock as actor when the reconcile pass fires them. No 'orchestrator' actor exists (understand N3).
discoverA5mediumThe judge, resolver and triage workers are the 'worker' actor running a task of a given kind (understand A5).
discoverA6highThe event order follows understand N7 (idea states), N8 (task branch states building, verifying, ready, in_bundle, landed with side states conflicted, gate_failed, abandoned) and N9 (worktree states reserved, created, active, landing, landed, orphaned, rescued, removed).
discoverA7medium'Worktree landed' (nothing unique left) is folded into Task Branch Landed and Worktree Removed; it is not a separate event.
discoverA8lowFeature Opened happens after Assumptions Written for an idea with no --to, as the Features section says; the idea row records its feature at capture only for --to (H7).
discoverA9mediumThe fleetd command channel, request files while fleetd is down, and the herdr pane mapping are design-level transport; they are not on the board.
discoverA10highEvent count 82 is above the standard band (25 to 60). The design has 4 state machines (idea, task, task branch, worktree) plus feature integration; merging them further hides the language conflicts H4 and H6.
decomposeA1highThe 6 contexts are modules inside horch-core in 1 deployable unit and 1 team (understand N6). The boundaries are model boundaries, not process boundaries.
decomposeA2mediumThe verifier stays a module of task-execution because it reads and writes the same task states and the reap rule (04 S7) needs 1 transaction. Open decision D1.
decomposeA3mediumThe question aggregate (worker-question-asked to question-escalated) belongs to ideas, because the sub-orchestrator answers it against the idea's assumptions. Open decision D2.
decomposeA4mediumWorker profiles and adapters are their own context because of their rate of change and their credential rules, although the storm holds only 2 of their events (discover H14). Open decision D3.
decomposeA5mediumWorktree custody is its own context, not a part of integration, because the worktree lease and the no-loss rules differ from the branch landing rules. Open decision D4.
decomposeA6mediumThe ledger is infrastructure that fleet-runtime owns as the single writer. Each context owns the state transitions of its own aggregates; it is not a shared kernel.
decomposeA7lowOperator attention (cap-operator-attention) maps to ideas, because approvals, interview questions and question escalation live there. Task escalation (task-escalated) stays in task-execution and reaches the operator through the same inbox.
decomposeA8highTriage and resolver tasks are opened by integration but run as normal tasks in task-execution; integration asks task-execution for them.
decomposeA9mediumEach preservation row has 1 owning context, as listed in N3. The row texts come from the Preservation analysis of design.md.
strategizeA1mediumIdeas is classified supporting, not core (decision D1 is open). Its 24 events are the transitions of 1 fixed idea state machine; the judgment work (research, interview, assumptions, spec, plan) is done by the sub-orchestrator model, not by fleetd code. Scored diff 6, cplx 5.
strategizeA2mediumCore stays the minority: 2 of 6 subdomains (task-execution, integration). Ideas would make 3 of 6, which is half, not a minority (ticket rule for this run).
strategizeA3mediumThe 2 cores use domain-model: state rows are the truth, and the events table is the audit trail that the one door writes beside each row in the same transaction (design, Ledger, rule 1 One door). Decision D2 keeps the event-sourced reading open.
strategizeA4highFleet runtime is supporting, not generic. Its pane hosting (herdr) and host services (launchd, systemd, Windows service) are adopted and only wrapped, as understand N14 says. The single ledger writer, the command channel and the platform layer interface have no product to buy, so the subdomain as a whole is built.
strategizeA5mediumWorktree custody is supporting with medium investment. Its no-loss rule (rescue ref written and read back before any removal) is 1 invariant over a 8-state lifecycle, not an algorithm; a failure breaks G2, so it gets invariant tests and fault-injection tests.
strategizeA6highWorker profiles is supporting with medium investment because it owns the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY scrub (C2, an absolute operator rule). Its complexity is the rate of change of the agent CLIs, not domain rules.
strategizeA7highEvery subdomain has evolution custom: each has at least 1 custom capability. The commodity and product capabilities of fleet-runtime (host services, pane hosting) are adopted systems, not built parts.
